translationRepairs: The emperor saw that he was steady and substantial, fluent in argument, versed in legal precedent, and could dress Legalist practice in Confucian language; he delighted in him, and within a year Hong rose to Left Metropolitan Superintendent.

The emperor saw that he was steady and substantial, fluent in argument, versed in the affairs of law clerks, and trimmed these with Confucian learning; he delighted in him, and within a year Hong rose to Left Metropolitan Superintendent.

s0084 has 習文法吏事，緣飾以儒術: practiced in clerk-law affairs and ornamented with Confucian learning. “Legalist practice” invents a school label absent from the Chinese; the proposed wording restores that sense.
The execution of Zhufu Yan and Dong Zhongshu's banishment to Jiaoxi were Hong's work.
The killing of Zhufu Yan and Dong Zhongshu's transfer to Jiaoxi were Hong's work.
s0119 reads 殺主父偃，徙董仲舒膠西: kill Zhufu Yan and transfer Dong Zhongshu to Jiaoxi. 徙 is relocation/transfer; “banishment” overstates the source verb.

Hong's son Du inherited the marquisate; having been governor of Shanyang for more than ten years, an edict summoned Magistrate Shi Cheng of Juye to the Public Carriage office; Du detained him and did not dispatch him; sitting judgment he was sentenced to wall labor.

Hong's son Du inherited the marquisate; having been governor of Shanyang for more than ten years, an edict summoned Shi Cheng, magistrate of Juye, to the Public Carriage office; Du detained him and did not dispatch him; for this offense he was sentenced to wall labor.

In 度留不遣，坐論為城旦, 坐論 marks Du as convicted and sentenced for detaining the magistrate. “Sitting judgment” calques awkwardly and can be misread as Du judging someone else; the proposed gloss clarifies the agent.
At Luoyang he learned Er Kuan had the seal—and laughed aloud.
At Luoyang he learned Er Kuan held the post—and laughed aloud.
Context s0248 concerns the vacant 御史大夫; s0249’s 聞兒寬為之 means Er Kuan held that post. “Had the seal” invents seal imagery not in 為之.
The sovereign meant to wield both wen and wu and hunted talent as if starved for it—he fetched Mei Sheng with the herb-wheeled cart and caught his breath at the sight of Zhufu Yan.
The sovereign meant to wield both wen and wu and hunted talent as if starved for it—he fetched Mei Sheng with the rush-wheeled cart and caught his breath at the sight of Zhufu Yan.
蒲輪 is the rush/cattail-padded wheeled carriage for honored guests, not an herb-wheeled cart; “herb-wheeled” misreads 蒲.

Never did the dynasty gather talent so thickly: Hong, Dong, and Kuan for classical breadth; the Shi brothers for steadfast service; Ji An and Bu Shi for blunt loyalty; Han Anguo and Zheng Dangshi for lifting others; Zhao Yu and Zhang Tang for codifying law; Sima Qian and Xiangru for voice; jesters Dongfang Shuo and Mei Gao; debaters Yan Zhu and Zhu Maichen; calendar-makers Tang Dou and Luoxia Hong; the harmonist Li Yan'nian; the reckoner Sang Hongyang; envoys Zhang Qian and Su Wu; blades Wei Qing and Huo Qubing; regents Huo Guang and Jin Midi—and a cloud of names besides.

Never did the dynasty gather talent so thickly: Hong, Dong, and Kuan for classical breadth; the Shi brothers for steadfast service; Ji An and Bu Shi for blunt loyalty; Han Anguo and Zheng Dangshi for lifting others; Zhao Yu and Zhang Tang for codifying law; Sima Qian and Xiangru for voice; jesters Dongfang Shuo and Mei Gao; debaters Yan Zhu and Zhu Maichen; calendar-makers Tang Du and Luoxia Hong; the harmonist Li Yan'nian; the reckoner Sang Hongyang; envoys Zhang Qian and Su Wu; blades Wei Qing and Huo Qubing; regents Huo Guang and Jin Midi—and a cloud of names besides.
歷數則唐都 names Tang Du (都 dú/dū); “Tang Dou” misreads the given name 都.

Thus Han obtained men; at this time it was most flourishing: in Confucian elegance then Gongsun Hong, Dong Zhongshu, Er Kuan; in steadfast conduct then Shi Jian, Shi Qing; in plain straightforwardness then Ji An, Bu Shi; in advancing the worthy then Han Anguo, Zheng Dangshi; in fixing statutes then Zhao Yu, Zhang Tang; in literary composition then Sima Qian, Xiangru; in jest then Dongfang Shuo, Mei Gao; in repartee then Yan Zhu, Zhu Maichen; in calendrical reckoning then Tang Dou, Luoxia Hong; in harmonizing pitch then Li Yan'nian; in planning transport then Sang Hongyang; as envoys then Zhang Qian, Su Wu; as generals then Wei Qing, Huo Qubing; as testamentary appointees then Huo Guang, Jin Midi—the rest cannot be fully recorded.
